content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations aimed at improving outcomes for preterm births. These guidelines are accessible through their official repository. 2. WHO has provided evidence-based recommendations for managing common childhood conditions, including newborn health issues, dysentery, pneumonia, oxygen use and delivery, fever causes, severe acute malnutrition, and supportive care. 3. WHO has developed guidelines for maternal and newborn care to ensure a positive postnatal experience, emphasizing evidence-based practices. 4. WHO has also released recommendations for antenatal care to promote a positive pregnancy experience, focusing on interventions that improve maternal and fetal health. 5. WHO has outlined intrapartum care recommendations to enhance the childbirth experience, ensuring safety and well-being for both mother and child. 6. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (Second Edition) provides a comprehensive framework for creating evidence-based health guidelines. 7. A systematic review by Edmond and Strobel highlights global healthcare interventions for preterm or low birth weight infants, summarizing evidence from multiple studies. 8. WHO emphasizes the importance of declarations of interest in maintaining ethical standards in healthcare guideline development. 9. The DECIDE project (2011–2015) focused on improving decision-making in healthcare through evidence-based approaches. 10. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) system is a widely recognized framework for assessing the quality of evidence and strength of healthcare recommendations. 11. The GRADE-CERQual project group provides tools to assess the confidence in evidence from qualitative research, ensuring robust decision-making. 12. UNICEF's supply catalogue offers essential resources for maternal and child health, particularly in low-resource settings. 13. The International Medical Products Price Guide (2015 Edition) provides pricing information for essential medical products, aiding in cost-effective healthcare delivery. 14. WHO's compendium of innovative health technologies (2022) highlights tools and devices designed for low-resource settings to improve healthcare outcomes. 15. Reporting the effects of interventions in EPOC (Effective Practice and Organisation of Care) reviews ensures transparency and reliability in healthcare research. 16. A search filter developed by Prady et al. identifies equity-focused studies, streamlining the process of finding relevant research in healthcare. 17. Langlois et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on inequities in postnatal care in lowand middle-income countries, identifying barriers and solutions. 18. A qualitative meta-synthesis by Anderzen-Carlsson et al. explores parental experiences of providing skin-to-skin care for their newborns, emphasizing its emotional and physical benefits. 19. Smith et al. reviewed barriers and enablers to the adoption of kangaroo mother care (KMC) in health systems, focusing on caregiver perspectives. 20. The WHO Immediate KMC Study Group demonstrated that immediate kangaroo mother care significantly improves survival rates for low birth weight infants. 21. Mazumder et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial showing the positive impact of community-initiated kangaroo mother care on infant survival. 22. Sivanandan and Sankar performed a systematic review and meta-analysis on kangaroo mother care for preterm or low birth weight infants, confirming its benefits. 23. Blunt et al. identified 25-hydroxycholecalciferol as a biologically active metabolite of vitamin D3, highlighting its importance in neonatal health. 24. Mony et al. studied the scaling up of kangaroo mother care in Ethiopia and India, demonstrating its feasibility and effectiveness through multi-site implementation research. 25. Klemming et al. proposed a mother-newborn couplet care model to ensure zero separation for all newborns, translating theory into practice. 26. Arora et al. implemented a quality improvement initiative to increase the duration of kangaroo mother care for preterm twins in resource-limited settings. 27. Minot et al. explored strategies to increase early skin-to-skin contact for extremely low birth weight infants, emphasizing its critical role in neonatal care. 28. Calibo et al. described the scaling up of kangaroo mother care in the Philippines through policy, regulatory, and systems reform to improve birth practices. 29. Hendricks-Munoz and Mayers developed a neonatal nurse training program in kangaroo mother care, reducing barriers to its utilization in NICUs. 30. Kapoor et al. enhanced kangaroo mother care uptake through the implementation of an education protocol, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving neonatal outcomes. 31. Mondkar et al. evaluated the impact of a mother-baby-friendly initiative on human milk feeding for neonates, showing significant improvements in hospital settings. 32. WHO recommendations for the care of preterm or low birth weight infants emphasize evidence-based practices to improve survival and health outcomes. 33. Vesel et al. reported findings from the Ghana Newhints trial, promoting skin-to-skin care for low birth weight babies and demonstrating its effectiveness. 34. Requejo et al. assessed the coverage of interventions for reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health, identifying gaps and opportunities for improvement. 35. WHO's guideline on breastfeeding in maternity and newborn services provides comprehensive recommendations to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding. 36. Baker et al. analyzed the global rise in commercial milk formula consumption, discussing its determinants, dynamics, and consequences for infant and young child diets. 37. Neves et al. examined trends in the consumption of breast milk, formula, and animal milk by children under two years across 113 countries, highlighting significant changes over time. 38. Tyebally Fang et al. called for further evidence and guidance on human milk banking, emphasizing its potential benefits and challenges. 39. Quigley et al. compared formula milk with donor breast milk for feeding preterm or low birth weight infants, providing insights into their relative benefits and risks. 40. Chagwena et al. surveyed health workers in Zimbabwe on the acceptability of donor breast milk banking, identifying key attitudes and concerns. 41. Esquerra-Zwiers et al. explored the emotional tensions faced by mothers of preterm infants who consent to using pasteurized donor human milk. 42. Lubbe et al. investigated stakeholder attitudes toward donating and utilizing human breast milk, highlighting factors influencing acceptance and utilization. 43. Magowan et al. identified barriers and facilitators to the acceptability of donor human milk in Eastern Uganda, providing insights for improving its adoption. 44. Tyebally Fang et al. contributed to the development of global guidance on human milk banking, addressing critical issues and best practices. 45. Rochow et al. proposed targeted fortification of breast milk with fat, protein, and carbohydrates for preterm infants, optimizing their nutritional intake. 46. Agostoni et al. provided commentary on enteral nutrient supply for preterm infants, offering recommendations from the European Society of Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition. 47. Arslanoglu et al. discussed new concepts and recommendations for optimizing human milk fortification for preterm infants, emphasizing individualized approaches. 48. Imdad and Bhutta reviewed nutritional management strategies for low birth weight/preterm infants in community settings, focusing on developing world perspectives. 49. Klingenberg et al. conducted an international survey on enteral feeding practices for very preterm infants, identifying variations and best practices. 50. Brown et al. reviewed multi-nutrient fortification of human milk for preterm infants, summarizing evidence from systematic reviews. 51. Hendrickson discussed the use of preterm formula for very low birth weight infants, highlighting its role in neonatal nutrition. 52. Horbar et al. analyzed weight growth velocity and postnatal growth failure in infants weighing 501 to 1500 grams, providing data from 2000 to 2013. 53. Walsh et al. compared nutrient-enriched formula with standard formula for preterm infants, evaluating their impact on growth and development. 54. Pollitt et al. studied the stability of sucking behavior in infants and its relationship to intake during the first month of life, providing insights into feeding patterns. 55. Shulhan et al. reviewed current knowledge of necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants, focusing on the impact of different types of enteral nutrition products. 56. WHO recommendations for the care of preterm or low birth weight infants emphasize the importance of evidence-based feeding practices. 57. Fang et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on quality improvement initiatives to increase breastfeeding in preterm infants. 58. Kinshella et al. identified barriers and facilitators for early and exclusive breastfeeding in health facilities in Sub-Saharan Africa, providing recommendations for improvement. 59. Chitale et al. reviewed early enteral feeding for preterm or low birth weight infants, summarizing evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses. 60. Black and Aboud embedded responsive feeding within a theoretical framework of responsive parenting, emphasizing its importance for child development. 61. Glodowski et al. identified the rooting reflex as an infant feeding cue, providing practical insights for caregivers. 62. McCormick et al. compared ad libitum or demand/semi-demand feeding with scheduled interval feeding for preterm infants, evaluating their relative benefits. 63. Watson and McGuire reviewed responsive versus scheduled feeding for preterm infants, highlighting the advantages of responsive feeding. 64. Fry et al. conducted a systematic review of quality improvement initiatives related to cue-based feeding in preterm infants, identifying effective strategies. 65. Talej et al. reviewed responsive feeding for preterm or low birth weight infants, summarizing evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses. 66. Brown and Sweet discussed strategies for preventing necrotizing enterocolitis in neonates, emphasizing evidence-based interventions. 67. McKeown et al. examined the role of delayed feeding and feeding increments in necrotizing enterocolitis, providing insights into risk reduction. 68. Oddie et al. reviewed the slow advancement of enteral feed volumes to prevent necrotizing enterocolitis in very low birth weight infants. 69. Yang et al. explored fast feed advancement strategies for preterm infants, evaluating their safety and effectiveness.
